title: Juice Gets a Gravity Boost from Earth
summary:
How can a spacecraft speed up without burning lots of fuel? It can get help from a planet’s gravity. On September 28, the European Space Agency’s Juice spacecraft used Earth for just such a boost on its journey toward Jupiter.

This move is called a gravity assist. A carefully chosen path past a planet lets its gravity change a spacecraft’s speed and direction. Earth’s pull turned Juice’s path by 20 degrees and increased its speed by 3.5 kilometers per second.

At its closest point, Juice passed 8,640 kilometers above the Indian Ocean. Its monitoring cameras took a series of pictures. During the four weeks before the encounter, controllers needed just one small adjustment to its course.

Saving fuel matters. Juice will need fuel later for observations around Jupiter and its icy moons. The spacecraft is scheduled to make 35 close passes by Ganymede, Callisto and Europa.

Earth also served as a practice target for Juice’s science tools. Teams planned activities for its 10 instruments, including checks to make sure their measurements work as expected. Such checks are called calibration.

The team had to choose activities carefully. While Juice was in Earth’s shadow, it relied only on battery power. The visit also gave scientists a chance to learn how the instruments behave in space.

For Juice, a trip past home was both a helpful push and a rehearsal for the science ahead.
why_it_matters: The Earth visit helped Juice save fuel and gave teams a chance to check the instruments that will study Jupiter’s icy moons.
